s: Rectitude and Blessedness are described as powerful and are approached with homage and praises.
The Good Mind is the companion with whom the male and female Bountiful Immortals dwell together.
is_approached_for homage and praises Universal Weal and Immortality are approached for homage and praises.
is_approached_for homage and praises The Kine's Soul is approached for homage and praises.
A sacrificial homage praising Ahura Mazda, identified from beginning to end as praise used for sacrifice and homage.
Mãthra Spenta is the holy, bounteous word of reason, working within and for us, identified and praised through sacrifice, homage, propitiation, glorification, and earnest Yasna.
Hvaniratha is a Karshvar the speaker desires to approach with praise.

l: standing offices of the Mazdayasnian Faith, Visparad
s: Standing Mazdayasnian Faith offices are among the things the speaker desires to approach with praise.

Haomas are offerings presented to Ahura Mazda, Verethraghna, the Bountiful Immortals, good waters, souls, and the holy creation. They include Haoma-water, holy Haoma, and mixtures with milk and Hadhânaêpata; pressed correctly, they are offered in libation to Ahura Mazda and Zarathustra Spitama and produce abundance in cattle and men.
is_a waters [good] The good waters receive earnest Yasna and homage.
Ahura Mazda’s fire is announced and presented in celebration, with perfume and sacred offerings for sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise.
belongs_to Zarathustra Spitâma [the saint] The Fravashi of Zarathustra Spitâma receives announcement in the celebration for sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise.
House whose celebrations promote and benefit its growth, overcoming restrictions and harmful malice while blessing household, herds, and retainers born and yet to be born.

The saints do good deeds, serve the renovation of the completed world, and have blessed Fravashis. Some are within and some outside the Province. Through their Fravashis and souls they receive offerings, announcements, and honors, and they and their Fravashis are worshipped.
The Avesta is a holy offering directed by Ahura Mazda and Zarathustra Spitâma, whose lawful, legitimate form and ritual prescripts are understood and declared by a priest.
Victory is a benefit for souls’ sanctification and well-being, unfolding as a reward of memorised recitals of good thoughts, words, and deeds.
Religious wisdom resides in sacred words, utterances, ceremonies, and ritual practices; its many teachings are correctly performed, imparted, and pondered.
Two mortars pour out Haomas, are pushed forward precisely, then turned and advanced toward wisest meaning.
Ritual deeds are wise offerings in the creation, delivered by Ahura Mazda, nourished by Vohu Manah and grown through Righteous Order, containing precepts with many meaningful incitations.

is_in Spenta Mainyu's world [among those who impart them to the chosen] The precepts are described as containing the wisest meaning and incitations. They are imparted to the chosen within Spenta Mainyu's world.
is_a being [among the greatest, best, and most beautiful] Vohu Manah is described as providing nourishment for the ritual deeds.
Spenta Mainyu's world is where the speakers seek to be while imparting precepts and incitations of the wisest meaning.

Visparad XIII (Sp. XV) sets out ritual worship and sacrifice to Ahura Mazda, the Bountiful Immortals, the sacrificial word correctly spoken, every Mãthra, Zarathustra, the blessings for the saints, and the hail addressed to the Bountiful Immortals. It also honors the three principal chapters and their parts without addition or omission.
Mãthra is a sacred word of reason, receives sacrifice, and is especially possessed by Zarathustra.
The three principal chapters are uttered and worshipped wholly; their Hâs, metrical lines, words, structure, recital, memorising, chanting, and offering are honored.

Visparad XIV (Sp. XVI). presents worship and sacrifice to Ahura Mazda, the Gâtha Ahunavaiti, and the Ahuna-vairya. It also describes the constituent parts and qualities associated with the Gâtha Ahunavaiti.

has_passages_identical_to Visp. I X [sections 4 and 5 are identical with sections 6 and 7] Visparad XV instructs Zarathustrian Mazdayasnians to prepare themselves for lawful deeds, avoid unlawful and evil deeds, further husbandry, and render the needy rich. It calls for Sraosha to be present for the worship of Ahura Mazda and the service, memorisation, and recital of the Yasna Haptanghâiti.
The sacred Order is the standard in accordance with which Zarathustrian Mazdayasnians are to perform lawful deeds.
Lawful deeds accord with the sacred Order and are enjoined through memorised recitals for Zarathustrian Mazdayasnians’ well-doing.
Worship is offered to Ahura Mazda, the Amesha Spenta, the holy man, the prior world of the holy and the clean, states of salvation and blessedness, and eternal salvation.
It is the unit in which striving after the good thoughts, words, and deeds of the Yasna Haptanghâiti is stated, along with a blessing concerning the Right (called) the Best and weal.
A brief statement affirms existence, including for a man directed toward Righteousness Best and right.

l: state of weal and salvation, Visparad
s: is_for holy man The state of weal and salvation for the holy man is worshipped.
Life-long blessedness is worshipped for the holy, while it unfolds as calamity for the evil man.
Eternal salvation belongs to evil man and is worshipped with salvation prayer.
Saints existing, now coming into existence, or future receive sacrifice throughout all times.
Visparad XIX (Sp. XXII) worships and sacrifices to Ahura Mazda, the Bountiful Immortals, Âramaiti, holy creatures, the sun, and other bountiful or holy realities.
Holy creatures are sacrificed to and worshipped, with intelligence or Righteousness first, associated with Âramaiti and the Righteous Order.
A shining sun, highest of the high, is worshipped with the Bountiful Immortals and Mãthras with good ceremonies.
Visparad XX (Sp. XXIII) presents sacrifices and worship offered to the Vohu-khshathra, the Khshathra-vairya, and the later Yasna, the heroic Haptanghâiti.
A good kingdom, Khshathra-vairya, receives sacrifice and encompasses rewards, health, healing, progress, growth, and victorious smiting.
Khshathra-vairya is the desired kingdom, identified as such and honored through sacrifice.
The correctly spoken sacrificial words are said to hold the Daêvas subject.
The Vahistôisti is named as the other point between which the listed rewards, health, healing, progress, growth, and victorious smiting are found.

l: memorised recital of the good thoughts, good words, and good deeds, Visparad
s: The memorised recital of good thoughts, good words, and good deeds brings rewards, health, healing, progress, growth, and victorious smiting, unfolding through resistance to evil and undoing treacherous, false, and unfair acts.
A Yasna defined by its offering, unfolding as a text that offers sacrifice to the later Yasna.
Visparad XXI concerns earnest Yasna and homage to good beings and sacrifice to forms of listening, mercy, praise, and the later Yasna.
Fertile fruit-trees bear fruit as of themselves and receive earnest Yasna and homage.
Visparad XXII (Sp. XXV) contains a chant and describes its associated ceremonial actions and supplications for the Kine.
The chant is fully chanted for Bountiful Immortals and holy Saoshyants, recognized by saint as fruitful of blessed gifts, but unknown to sinner.

This document collects Zoroastrian ritual texts: Âfrînagân services, the five Gâhs, and miscellaneous fragments. Âfrînagân blesses Hâvani, seasonal lords, the Gâthas, and Rapithwina; it requires Mazdayasnians to bring Myazda or substitutes, imposes expulsion and penance for failure, and seeks rulers’ strength, victory, health, long life, and Heaven. The Gâhs organize sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise across five ritual times, invoking Ahura Mazda, Zarathustra, fires, Fravashis, and divine powers while rejecting the Daêvas. The fragments broaden this ritual order through instructions, confessions, prayers, and moral teaching: good thoughts, words, and deeds lead to Heaven, evil ones to Hell. They praise sacred beings and powerful words, and call for the defeat of Angra Mainyu, the Daêvas, and the Drug(k).

l: Âfrînagân, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a ritual collection Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] Âfrînagân contains sections for Gahanbâr, Gâtha, and Rapithvin observances. It prescribes offerings, blessings, disciplinary measures, and ritual procedures.

l: Ahura Mazda, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Ahura Mazda is a worshipped, radiant and glorious Lord: the holy, highest object of ritual order. He is propitiated, worshipped, sacrificed to, praised, and associated with Sovereign Power. He is creator of the waters, father of Fire, and ruler over his creatures. His Kingdom belongs to him and offers a nurturer to the poor. He grants or declares rewards and ritual instructions, and declares his sovereign rule from beginning to end.

l: Zarathustra, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Zarathustra is a saint, founder, model, and order-giver of the Mazda-worshippers. He keeps company with Good Mind, Righteousness the Best, and Khshathra-vairya as incitations to priests or worshippers. Ahura Mazda speaks to him, and he asks about the reward for performing the Rapithwina ritual. Sacrifice is offered to him, his Fravashi, words, and deeds. Zarathustra Spitama is instructed to declare words for sacrifice and worship to his male and female disciples.

l: Daêvas, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: must_disappear earth [likewise] The Daêvas are commanded to disappear beneath the earth. Their disappearance is associated with the unhindered arising of the dead and the sustaining of bodily life.

l: Mazdayasnians, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Mazdayasnians assemble for ritual service, oppose the Daêvas, and must offer service and appropriate Myazda or risk expulsion.

l: Gâh Hâvan, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Gâh Hâvan is the first Gâh, concerning Hâvani and other holy beings. Hâvani, holy lord and regulator of ritual order, presides in daylight at Hâvani’s appointed time. The service offers sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise, including sacrifice to the five Gâthas and to Zarathustra’s words and deeds.

l: Righteousness the Best, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Righteousness the Best is Ritual Righteousness, a lofty holy lord of the ritual order. It receives worship, homage, propitiation, praise, and sacrifice; is the best blessing, weal, and right conduct; and is identified with Asha Vahista, associated with Ahura Mazda's Fire and blessings.

l: Maidhyô-zaremya, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a lord Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] Maidhyô-zaremya is named as a lord to whom propitiation, homage, and praise are offered. Its Myazda consists of sound flesh from a choice beast with a full flow of milk, or an equivalent substitute when necessary.

l: Myazda, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Myazda is a ritual offering for six seasonal observances, beginning with Maidhyô-zaremya; failure to bring it can bring expulsion and expiating deeds.

l: Ratu, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Ratu is a ruler who guides disciples, receives required Myazda, expels those who fail to bring it, may impose expiating deeds, and receives wood when the prescribed offering cannot be made.

l: Heaven, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: belongs_to good thoughts, words, and deeds [as the best world] Heaven is described as the home of those who think good thoughts, speak good words, and do good deeds. It is called the best world.

l: Âfrîn[-Agân] Gâtha, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a Gâtha Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] Âfrîn[-Agân] Gâtha praises Ahura Mazda, the Bountiful Immortals, and the holy Gâthas. It offers propitiation to the Fravashis of the saints and sacrifice to the five named Gâthas.

l: the Bountiful Immortals, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: The Bountiful Immortals are holy beings and guardians of the saints. They receive praise, propitiation, invocation, and sacrifice in Âfrîn[-Agân] Gâtha, Rapithvin, and ritual instruction. Possessing words declared for sacrifice and worship, they rule and dispose of all things aright, and gather for assembly and reunion on the heights of Heaven.

l: lofty Gâthas, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: are_a ritual powers [bountiful and holy; ruling in the ritual order] Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] The Gâthas are called bountiful and holy and are said to rule in the ritual order. Ahunavaiti, Ustavaiti, Spentâ-mainyu, Vohu-khshathra, and Vahistôisti each receive sacrifice.

l: Fravashis of the saints, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: belong_to saints [mighty and overwhelming] The Fravashis of the saints receive sacrifice and homage as the good, heroic, and bountiful Fravashis of saints, including those of the living, the dead, the bodily, and those in heaven. They are also invoked in connection with the holy woman, prosperity, and the good order.

l: Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a ritual text Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin concerns Rapithwina, its associated ritual lords, and the reward for performing the Rapithwina office. It records Ahura Mazda's answer to Zarathustra about the merit of the properly conducted observance.

l: Gâh Rapithvin, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Gâh Rapithvin is a holy lord and ritual time within the ritual order, associated with Frâdat-fshu and Zantuma. It includes five Gâthas, each holy and ruling in that order. Its blessing and office unfold through ritual acts with washed hands, Baresman, Haoma, fire, and spoken Ahuna-vairya, binding tongue and body to Mãthra. It is devoted to Rapithwina, associated lords, Asha Vahista, and Ahura Mazda's Fire, while invoking Gâthas, words, waters, lands, plants, Fravashis, and the Bountiful Immortals' assembly.

l: Zantuma, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Zantuma is a holy lord of the ritual order, named alongside Frâdat-fshu and honored with sacrifice, worship, and homage among the Bountiful Immortals.

l: Fire, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Fire, Ahura Mazda’s son and holy lord of ritual order, receives sacrifice and praise, is associated with Asha Vahista, and brings blessing.

l: the Rapithwina office, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_performed_with the Rapithwina blessing Gahanbâr. .. III. Âfrîn[-Agân] Rapithvin.] The Rapithwina office is recited and performed with the Rapithwina prayer for blessing and the prescribed ritual preparations. The person who performs it properly receives a reward like the southern wind that advances, increases, blesses, rejoices, and causes the material world to progress.

l: Ahuna-vairya, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: A revered prayer, chosen by Mazda, unfolds as words belonging to Mazda and counted among victorious sacred words.

l: the Rapithwina ritual, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: The Rapithwina ritual requires prepared hands, mortars, Baresman, Haoma, fire, recitation, tongue, and body; properly performed, it earns Ahura Mazda’s declared reward.

l: The Gâhs, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a ritual sections The Gâhs comprise five ritual sections: Gâh Hâvan, Gâh Rapithvin, Gâh Uziren, Gâh Aiwisrûthrima, and Gâh Ushahin. They prescribe sacrifice, homage, propitiation, praise, and blessing for Ahura Mazda and numerous holy lords of the ritual order.

l: Gâh Uziren, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a holy lord of the ritual order Gâh Uziren concerns Uzayêirina, Frâdat-vîra, Dahvyuma, Apãm-napât, and the waters created by Mazda. It sacrifices to the ritual officiants, celestial bodies, later lore, the creation by day and night, Fire, and the water which Mazda created.

l: Gâh Aiwisrûthrima, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a holy lord of the ritual order Gâh Aiwisrûthrima concerns Aiwisrûthrima, Aibigaya, Frâdat-vîspãm-hugyâiti, and Zarathustrôtema. It invokes Fravashis, women who have many sons, prosperity, strength, the victorious Blow, the sacred vows, social leaders, the house-mistress, and exemplary holy men and women.

l: Gâh Ushahin, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Gâh Ushahin is a holy lord of the ritual order, concerned with Ushahina, Beregya, Nmânya, Sraosha, Rashnu, and Arstât; it sacrifices to Aurora, dawn, Ahura Mazda, Good Mind, Asha Vahista, Khshathra-vairya, and Âramaiti, then blesses Sraosha, Rashnu, and Arstât.

l: Mithra of the wide pastures, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a Yazad [of the spoken name; of the thousand ears and myriad eyes] Mithra of the wide pastures is described as having a thousand ears and a myriad eyes. He receives sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise, especially in connection with Vîsya and Râman Hvâstra.

l: Râman Hvâstra, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a ritual recipient Râman Hvâstra receives sacrifice, homage, propitiation, and praise alongside Mithra of the wide pastures. He is also invoked for the worship and exaltation of Vîsya.

l: Airyemâ-ishyô, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Airyemâ-ishyô is a holy, authoritative prayer, proclaimed greatest and most helpful for progress; it is revered and urged for use by the Saoshyants.

l: the five Gâthas, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a Mãthra [surpassing] The five Gâthas are described as a surpassing Mãthra invoked through Airyemâ-ishyô. The Gâh Rapithvin names the Gâthas Ahunavaiti, Ustavaiti, Spentâ-mainyu, Vohu-khshathra, and Vahistôisti as holy and ruling in the ritual order.

l: Apãm-napât, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Apãm-napât is a lofty, royal Ahura and brilliant lord of the waters created by Mazda, with fleet horses. He is invoked and addressed as sacrifices, homage, propitiation, praise, and blessing are offered to him.

l: Dahvyuma, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a holy lord of the ritual order Dahvyuma is named as a holy lord of the ritual order alongside Frâdat-vîra. Sacrifice is offered to him in connection with the manifest performance and fulfillment of truth, later lore, and the creation by day and night.

l: Sraosha, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Sraosha is Obedience, blessed and recompensed or sanctified, who smites victoriously, advances and increases settlements, and receives sacrifice and blessing in Gâh Ushahin.

l: Rashnu, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Rashnu, a major entity and most just judge, receives sacrifice in Gâh Ushahin and is included in its final blessing.

l: Arstât, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: causes_settlements_to_advance settlements [and to increase] Arstât is described as causing the settlements to advance and increase. He receives sacrifice and is included with Sraosha and Rashnu in the final blessing.

l: Khshathra-vairya, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Khshathra-vairya is named with the Good Mind and Righteousness the Best. It is also identified as the Kingdom to be desired and is invoked against the Drug(k).

l: Miscellaneous Fragments, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: is_a document unit The Miscellaneous Fragments contain ritual directions, prayers, praises, confessions, moral teachings, and invocations concerning Mazda-worship and the defeat of evil.

l: Thraêtaona, the Âthwyan, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Thraêtaona, the Âthwyan, is a saint and holy lord of the ritual order. He is praised and worshipped; offerings of propitiation, sacrifice, homage, strength, and swiftness go to his saintly Fravashi, while ordered sacrificers are protected from Kuro, Tarewani, and Karpan.

l: Hell, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Hell is identified as the place where those who think, speak, and do evil thoughts, words, and deeds abide.

l: good thoughts, words, and deeds, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Good thoughts, words, and deeds performed with intelligence lead their thinkers, speakers, and doers to Heaven, the best world.

l: evil thoughts, words, and deeds, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Evil thoughts, words, and deeds are performed with folly, and those who do them are assigned Hell.

l: Angra Mainyu, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: must_be_hidden_beneath earth Angra Mainyu is contrasted with Ahura Mazda as a ruler over realms. He is commanded to be hidden beneath the earth, and no one is to rule as Angra Mainyu over Ahura Mazda’s realms.

l: Ahurian One of Ahura, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: receives sacrifice [water which Mazda created] The Ahurian One of Ahura is addressed as the water which Mazda created. Praises, sacrifices, deeds of adoration, and offerings are directed to this being.

l: Drug(k), Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: Drug(k) is a malignant, sinful force causing seasonal moons to wane; she advances armed and strong, but is destroyed after Khshathra is with the speaker.

l: Mãthra-spenta word, Afrinagan, Gahs and Miscellaneous Fragments
s: The Mãthra-spenta word is unsubdued, undeceived, victorious, opposed to malice, and healing; when pronounced, it gives great victory to its utterer.

This sequence from the Vendidad presents Ahura Mazda’s teachings to Spitama Zarathustra, beginning with creation and ending in detailed rules for purity and atonement. In Fargard I, Ahura Mazda lists beautiful lands he created, including Airyana Vaêgô, Sughdha, Môuru, and Bâkhdhi, while Angra Mainyu counters each with evils such as serpents, sin, and winter. Fargard II turns to Yima, who declines to receive the law but agrees to protect the material world; after enlarging the overcrowded earth three times, he builds the Vara to preserve selected people, animals, plants, and fires from fatal winters. Zarathustra and Urvatad-nara rule there, and Karshipta brings Mazda’s law. The following units establish religious and social order. Fargard III explains what delights or grieves the Earth: worship, households, cultivation, herds, and care for the faithful are good, while corpses, Dakhmas, fiendish burrows, and captivity bring grief. It also connects confession and Mazda’s law with cleansing sin. Fargard IV regulates contracts, breaches, assault, restitution, and escalating penalties, including severe punishment for lying before truth-knowing water. Fargards V through VIII concentrate on death pollution, especially the Drug Nasu, and on protecting water, fire, land, people, animals, and sacred things. They prescribe where bodies and bones may be placed, how polluted ground and objects are treated, how corpses are removed from water or secured from it, and how people, clothing, utensils, animals, food, and places are cleansed. They include rules for still-born children, Dakhmas, healers and their payments, sexual conduct, and confession. The final record specifically addresses a fire used to burn a corpse, its dispersal, rewards for bringing fire to the Dâityô-gâtu, and cleansing a corpse-touched person with gômêz, water, running, and assistance, alongside further penalties and atonements.

Ahura Mazda is a creator and Maker of the material world, described as holy, most beneficent Spirit and Holy One, and as the father of Fire. He makes the good lands and countries dear to their dwellers, is highly renowned in Airyana Vaêgô by the good river Dâitya, and governs life-giving waters: sending water from sea Vouru-kasha with wind and clouds, bringing it to Dakhma, returning it unseen to sea Pûitika, and raining plants upon the earth for food and fodder. He teaches the law of Ahura, first conversing with Yima and instructing him to nourish, rule, protect the material world, and build the Vara against overcrowding and fatal winters. He then speaks with Spitama Zarathustra, answering questions about the Earth, happiness and grief, cultivation, food, sin, contracts, corpses, dead matter, water, fire, purity, pollution, the Drug Nasu, healing, sexual conduct, and the Daêva. His teaching supplies detailed rules for cultivation, confession and cleansing, contracts, atonements, penalties, treatment and removal of the dead, Dakhmas, purification, and protection from defilement. Across the records, he establishes the world’s lands and sustenance, gives law and guidance, and repeatedly answers questions by prescribing order, cleansing, rewards, and penalties.

Zarathustra is a mortal, righteous and holy recipient of Ahura Mazda’s teachings, identified as the first mortal taught the law after Yima. Across the records, Ahura Mazda addresses him, often as Spitama Zarathustra, and explains created lands, their counter-created evils, the Earth, cultivation, food, corpses, and Mazda’s law. Zarathustra increasingly asks about death, ritual purity, dead matter, water, fire, pollution, cleansing, healing, Dakhmas, fiends, bones, and still-born children. The account unfolds as a sustained teaching and questioning exchange about law, mortality, and proper treatment of the dead.

l: the good lands and countries, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: are_made_dear_to the whole living world [through their dwellers] The good lands and countries were created by Ahura Mazda, beginning with Airyana Vaêgô and continuing through sixteen named lands. They are described as beautiful, deep, desirable, bright, and thriving.

Airyana Vaêgô is the first created good land and country, lying by the good river Dâitya. Angra Mainyu brings a serpent into the river and winter with severe plagues, leaving ten winter months and two summer months. By Dâitya, Ahura Mazda gathers celestial gods, and Yima gathers excellent mortals.

l: the good river Dâitya, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Dâitya, the good river in Airyana Vaêgô, is where Ahura Mazda and Yima call their respective meetings.

Angra Mainyu is all death. By witchcraft, he counter-creates harmful beings, sins, conditions, the serpent in the river, and winter in lands made by Ahura Mazda; he is also associated with brands on mortal bodies, which are absent from the Vara.

Fatal winters are a work of the Daêvas and a counter-creation of Angra Mainyu, foretold by Ahura Mazda. They come upon the material world with fierce, foul frost and deep snow, bringing winter’s worst plagues and causing all three sorts of beasts to perish.

l: the plains in Sughdha, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The plains in Sughdha, the second good land and country created by Ahura Mazda, faced Angra Mainyu’s death-bringing fly Skaitya.
Selected seeds of sheep, oxen, and every kind of cattle are brought into the Vara. The cattle remain there with the preserved men, women, plants, birds, and fires.

l: the strong, holy Môuru, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Môuru, the third good land created, was countered by sinful lusts through Angra Mainyu’s witchcraft.

l: the beautiful Bâkhdhi with high-lifted banners, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Bâkhdhi, a beautiful good land with high-lifted banners, was fourth created; Angra Mainyu counter-created the Bravara there.

l: the burning of corpses, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Burning corpses is an unforgivable sin, punished by death; its fire is dispersed and its cauldron and tripod removed, though bringing it to Dâityô-gâtu earns fire-brands.

Yima, son of Vîvanghat and a great shepherd, rules the material world with golden implements. First mortal to converse with Ahura Mazda, he declines to preach the law, enlarges the overcrowded earth, and builds the Vara to preserve selected life from fatal winters.

l: law of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The law of Mazda is a holy law belonging to Mazda, taught by Ahura Mazda to Yima before Zarathustra; Yima refuses to preach or bear it. It is fulfilled and strengthened through worship, sowing corn, holiness, and cleansing oneself with good thoughts, words, and deeds. For one who confesses sin and resolves not to repeat forbidden deeds, it removes sin and cleanses every evil thought, word, and deed. It is a fiend-destroying law, greater, better, and fairer than other utterances.
Ahura Mazda creates the material world, places it under Yima’s care, and warns that fatal winters will bring frost, snow, and destruction of beasts.

Earth is a material world. Under Yima’s sway it is replenished with flocks and herds and enlarged in successive expansions, becoming full of flocks, herds, men, dogs, birds, and red blazing fires. It is happiest where the faithful worship and cultivate it, where households, cattle, wife, children, and good herds thrive, and where increase and dung abound. It grieves at Arezûra, corpses, Dakhmas, burrows of Angra Mainyu’s creatures, and captivity of the faithful’s families. It rejoices when corpses and Dakhmas are removed, burrows filled, land tilled, and produce given to the faithful.

is_a royal implement [used by Yima] Ahura Mazda gives Yima a golden ring and a gold-inlaid poniard as signs of royal sway. Yima uses the golden ring to press and enlarge the earth, and later seals the Vara with it.

Men are among the beings that multiply until there is no more room on the earth. Selected men are brought into the Vara, where they live the happiest life. Men are included among those whose deaths require the ground to lie fallow for a year. Dead men are also included in the bones and bodies whose placement on the ground incurs penalties.

Dog is an animal whose death can require a year of fallow ground and purification, especially when it dies under a house or hut. Its body may incur penalties when placed on the ground. Ritual yellow or white forms are led along a corpse-bearing way to drive away Drug Nasu, and corpse-eating dogs may smite Nasu.

Vara is a square enclosure made by Yima as an abode for men and a fold for flocks. It holds flowing water, selected men and women, cattle, trees, fruit, birds, dwellings, and seeds, all of the finest kinds. It excludes Angra Mainyu’s brands, divides into parts with nine, six, and three streets, and is sealed with a golden ring, with a door, self-shining window, and lights.

Water is a divine witness: brimstoned, golden, and truth-knowing. It kills no man, though Astô-vîdhôtu, Vaya, the flood, birds, and chance are connected with death. It flows to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones, then returns through the sea Pûitika cleansed. Corpse-contact makes water unclean and unfit to drink until removal and required drawing off, melting, flowing, or passing intervals restore it. It purifies clothing, wood, corn, eating vessels, a cow, and man, with gômêz and earth where prescribed. It is kept from graves, sprinkled from skull to feet, and requires atonement when found by a man who touched a corpse.

l: men and women (Vara), Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The Vara receives seeds of the greatest, best, and finest men and women; every fortieth year, each couple has a male and female child who live happiest lives.
Karshipta, a bird, brings the law of Mazda and Ahura into the Vara made by Yima.
is_lord_and_ruler_of Vara [with Zarathustra] Urvatad-nara is named by Ahura Mazda as the lord and ruler in the Vara, together with Zarathustra.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The worshippers of Mazda worship Ahura Mazda and follow and fulfill Mazda’s law through love, beseeching, holy objects, priests, families, herds, and cultivation. They cultivate Earth, corn, grass, and fruit abundantly, may receive produce, and face captivity of wife and children. They must keep corpses at prescribed distances, find a Dakhma, handle and move dead bodies, purify houses, recite fiend-smiting words, and are cleansed from evil thought, word, and deed.

l: worshippers of Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The worshippers of Mazda are a group governed by rules for the dead, polluted ground, cleansing, healing, and offerings. They construct houses for the dead, lay corpses on the Dakhma, observe waiting periods before returning to fire, and handle a still-born child and mother through required distances, food, confinement, and washing. Where dogs or men have died, they leave the ground fallow for a year, may sow and water only the rest, and are subject to Peshôtanus if they violate this. They inspect and cleanse affected ground, remove corpses from water, secure corpses, and provide places for bones. Healing with the knife requires proven treatment of worshippers of the Daêvas.

Fire is a sacred witness and son of Ahura Mazda. It destroys thousands of unseen Daêvas, fiends, Yâtus, and Pairikas wherever sweet-smelling woods’ perfume travels. It does not kill a man: Astô-vîdhôtu and Vaya carry him off, then Fire burns life and limb. It must be removed after death, kept from graves and corpse-bearing ways, and returned or permitted after prescribed rites.
Fiends gather at Dakhmas, feed and void filth on corpses, and through stench cause and strengthen disease.
The Drug, a fiend, is assailed with fiend-smiting words and commanded to perish, flee north, and no longer give the living world to death.

A corpse after death is assaulted by the Drug Nasu and pollutes people, objects, and ground; recovery may take a year or fifty years. It may be burned, while a man touching it can be cleansed by stated procedures.

The Dakhma is a place on the earth where worshippers of Mazda lay corpses, with the eyes toward the sun, for exposure. Rain falls on its exposed corpse and unclean remains. Fiends gather and feed there, bringing pollution and disease. Ahura Mazda urges people to pull down Dakhmas, and worshippers seek one when a dog or man dies under a house or hut.

Drug Nasu is a polluting, corpse-associated defiling fiend, appearing as a raging fly. It rushes forth when a person or certain dogs die, comes from and is driven toward northern regions, and spreads infection, pollution, and uncleanness. Its defilement varies with the dead person’s status, affecting nearby beings, people resting together, corpses, bedding, clothing, and water; a priest’s death defiles ten and a warrior’s nine. It pollutes ponds, wells, snow, hail, and running water when a corpse is present, with specified purification. After death it rushes upon a dead man, and it also attacks those who eat corpses or bring corpses with filth into water or fire. Dogs, birds, water, and fiend-smiting words can drive or smite it. In cleansing, water drives it down the body until it leaves through the toes and soles toward the north; whether corpse-eating dogs or birds smote it affects the required number of washes.

Aspahê-astra is an implement of punishment used for prescribed stripes: penalties run from five for a first Âgerepta to a thousand for broken contracts, including four hundred stripes as atonement for a man who touched a corpse.

The Sraoshô-karana is an implement of punishment used with the Aspahê-astra for prescribed stripes, with numbers set by offenses and a four-hundred-stripe atonement for a corpse-toucher who encounters water or trees.

Corn is food: sown, it fulfills the law of Mazda and increases holiness; coming forth with barley and wheat, it destroys Daêvas; eaten, it gives strength for holiness, husbandry, and begetting children.

l: cultivation of the earth, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: is_required_for food [as a source of material sustenance] Cultivation involves tilling the Earth with the left and right arms, watering dry ground, drying wet ground, and growing corn, grass, and fruit. The Earth rewards the cultivator with people seeking bread and abundant food, while the uncultivated person must beg at a stranger's door.

l: burial of corpses, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Burial of a dog’s or man’s corpse requires disinterment within half a year or increasing stripes; if left into the second year, professors or students of Mazda’s law receive no payment, atonement, or cleansing.

Sin is a wrong that may be removed or atoned for through repentance, confession, and a resolve not to repeat the deed. Under the law of Mazda, confession can remove many sins and penalties, including grave deeds, and may apply even to those not taught in that law. Yet some deeds are stated to have no atonement, including voluntary emission of seed under the stated rule.

Atonement is required for contract-breaking, certain repeated assaults, confessed sin, and a corpse-toucher who encounters water or trees. Contract penalties increase from three hundred-fold for a word-contract to a thousand-fold for a field-contract; unatoned or refused repeated assaults bring Peshôtanu status and stripes. Confession under Mazda’s law can effect full atonement, while voluntary seed emission by those taught the law has none. The corpse-toucher’s atonement is eight hundred stripes split between two instruments.

is_provided_by law of Mazda [for the faithful] Cleansing is performed through gômêz and water, with prescribed stages and bodily washing after contact with a corpse. The law of Mazda also cleanses the faithful from every evil thought, word, and deed.

Punishments include stripes with the Aspahê-astra and the Sraoshô-karana. They range from thirty stripes with each instrument for a small bone to one thousand stripes with each instrument for a whole body, with two hundred stripes each for several other offenses.
Fargard IV establishes six contracts, penalties for breaches, classifications of violence and assault, and severe consequences for repeated offenses and falsehood.
A borrower who keeps a neighbour’s property after return is requested steals the lender; related wrongdoing can bring escalating stripes and Peshôtanu status.
The word-contract is the first and lowest of six contracts; breaking it requires redemption by the hand-contract and brings a three hundred-fold atonement with specified stripes.
The hand-contract, second of six contracts, redeems a broken word-contract; if broken, the sheep-contract redeems it through six hundred-fold atonement and six hundred stripes with each implement.
The sheep-contract, third of six contracts, redeems a broken hand-contract; if broken, the ox-contract redeems it with seven hundred-fold atonement and seven hundred stripes per instrument.
The ox-contract, fourth of six contracts, redeems a broken sheep-contract; if broken, the man-contract redeems it with eight hundred-fold atonement and stripes.
The man-contract, fifth of six contracts, redeems a broken ox-contract; if broken, the field-contract redeems it with nine hundred-fold atonement and stripes.
The field-contract is the sixth and highest contract, concerning good, fruitful, productive land; breaking it brings thousand-fold atonement and a thousand stripes with each implement.

Contract-breaking is a sin. Its atonement and stripe penalties rise by instrument: three hundred-fold for the word-contract, then six, seven, eight, and nine hundred-fold for hand, sheep, ox, and man contracts, ending at a thousand-fold for the field-contract.

Âgerepta is an act of rising to smite a man. Its penalty begins at five stripes with each implement, rises to ninety by the seventh occurrence, and ends at two hundred stripes when an eighth offense is unatoned or atonement is refused.

An Avaoirista is the act of coming upon a man to smite him. Penalties begin at ten stripes with each implement, rise to ninety by the sixth occurrence, and reach two hundred when a seventh occurrence is unatoned or atonement is refused.

Aredus is the act of actually smiting a man with evil aforethought. Its punishment begins at fifteen stripes with each instrument and rises to ninety by the fifth occurrence; a sixth unatoned occurrence or refusal to atone makes the offender Peshôtanu, liable to two hundred stripes.

is_a offender [designation after the specified repeated or unatoned offense] A Peshôtanu is the status assigned when specified assaults are repeated without atonement or when the offender refuses to atone. The penalty stated for this status is two hundred stripes with the Aspahê-astra and two hundred with the Sraoshô-karana.

l: violence and bodily assault, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: has_penalty two hundred stripes [repeated or unatoned assault, with each implement] Violence is classified as Âgerepta, Avaoirista, or Aredus according to whether a man rises to strike, approaches to strike, or strikes with evil aforethought. Bodily assaults receive escalating penalties: striking and seriously hurting another, causing blood, breaking a bone, or causing death each leads to specified stripes, with repeated unatoned or refused offenses making the offender a Peshôtanu.

Ashemaogha is an ungodly wicked two-footed ruffian opposed by man, who while alive directly and indirectly defiles creatures of the good spirit by harming water, fire, the cow, and faithful people; when dead, he defiles no more than a long-dead dried-venom frog.

is_a sea The sea Vouru-kasha sends waters down with the wind and clouds to corpses, Dakhmas, unclean remains, and bones. The waters later return unseen from the sea Pûitika toward the well-watered tree.
Sea Pûitika receives returning waters, boils and cleanses them, then sends the cleansed waters back to sea Vouru-kasha.

l: law of Zarathustra, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The law of Zarathustra is a fiend-destroying law, greater than other utterances in greatness, goodness, and fairness, allowing specified remission through authorities and repentance.
is_a greatest good [next to life] Purity is described as the greatest good for man next to life. It is procured by the law of Mazda through good thoughts, words, and deeds.

A man may die under a house, with prescribed treatment of house and body. Contact with a corpse can require gômêz then water cleansing, while specified sexual acts, covering a corpse, and voluntary seed emission incur consequences.

l: woman with child, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: A woman with child who delivers a still-born child is confined in a clean, dry enclosure of a Mazdean house, thirty paces from fire, water, and baresma and three from the faithful. She is unclean for three nights, follows prescribed food, and drinks gômêz mixed with ashes for three, six, or nine cups. After three nights she is cleaned with gômêz and water; she remains separated for nine nights and later washes her body and clothes.

A still-born child whose birth makes the woman who bears it unclean. During and after delivery, it requires her separation in an enclosure, with prescribed distances from fire, water, baresma, and the faithful, followed by stated purification periods.

A corpse is kept in a house for the dead, then laid on the Dakhma with its eyes toward the sun, where rain and birds act upon it and birds may eat it after death. It may be carried by dogs, birds, wolves, winds, or flies without sin. A corpse found in running water, ponds, wells, snow, or hail must be removed and laid on dry ground; until removal and purification, it makes portions of water unclean. It contaminates wood and corn, though these may be cleansed by separation and sprinkling. A dead body is removed from a house when possible, or the house is removed; it may remain in a grave until signs allow removal. After over a year dried and dead, man may touch it without impurity.

contains fire [before a death occurs there] A house containing the fire, baresma, cups, Haoma, and mortar must be cleared of those objects when a dog or man dies there. The fire may return after nine nights in winter or a month in summer, and a house with a woman who bears a still-born child must provide a clean enclosure at prescribed distances.

l: houses for the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Houses for the dead are three small structures raised in every house and borough after summer, each sized for a standing person and holding a lifeless body for two nights, three nights, or a month.

Gômêz is a purifying substance, mixed with ashes and used before or with water. It cleanses clothing, wood, corn, eating vessels, women after still-born delivery, cows that ate corpses, and people who touched or bore corpses. For corpse-bearers it comes from sheep or oxen; human urine is excluded except from the nearest kinsman or kinswoman of the dead. It is used to wash hair and bodies, then water completes cleansing.

Haoma touched by a corpse can be made clean. When strained for the Sacrifice, it is not corrupted or killed; when unstrained, four fingers’ length of its stem is defiled and must be buried in the ground for a year.

Ground where dogs or men have died lies fallow for a year, without sowing or watering. It is then inspected and made fit for tillage by removing bones, hair, flesh, dung, and blood. Ground exposed to a dead man recovers after one year; buried corpses require fifty years, and beneath a Dakhma recovery awaits mingled dust.

l: bones of the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Bones of dead dogs or men must be kept in a building beyond dogs, foxes, wolves, and rain-water; if a building cannot be afforded, they are laid on a carpet and pillow under open sky. Ground placement incurs escalating penalties.
A running stream is defiled around a corpse, three steps down, nine up, six across, then becomes clean after the corpse is removed and it flows three times.

is_built_with stones, mortar, and earth [when the worshippers of Mazda can afford it] A building for the bones of the dead should be beyond the reach of the dog, fox, and wolf and should not retain rain-water. It should be made with stones, mortar, and earth if the worshippers of Mazda can afford it.
A house containing a dead dog or man is perfumed or removed as easier, purified, then made clean and usable for preparing meals with meat and wine.
The bodies of the dead should be brought to the highest summits where corpse-eating dogs and corpse-eating birds are always known to be present.

l: death of dogs or men, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: The death of dogs or men requires the ground where the death occurred to remain fallow for a year. Sowing or watering that ground within the year is treated as bringing dead matter to water, earth, and plants.

l: sowing and watering ground, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: is_a sin [when performed within the year on ground where dogs or men have died] Worshippers of Mazda may sow and water the rest of the ground as they like, but not the part where dogs or men have died until a year has passed. Sowing or watering the defiled part within the year incurs the status of Peshôtanus and severe stripes.

l: removal of corpses from water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: requires laying the corpse on dry ground [after taking it out of the water] A person who encounters a corpse in running water must remove it after taking off shoes and clothes and entering the water as deeply as necessary. If the corpse is rotting, the person must draw out as much as can be grasped with both hands and lay it on dry ground.

l: pollution and purification of water, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Pollution by a corpse affects specified areas of ponds, snow or hail, and running streams, while wells remain unclean until the corpse is removed. Purification involves removing the corpse and drawing off part of the water, melting snow or hail, or allowing a stream to flow three times.

l: burial and securing of the dead, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: takes_place_on high summits [where corpse-eating dogs and corpse-eating birds are always known to be] The dead should be placed on high summits and fastened by the feet and hair with brass, stones, or lead so dogs and birds cannot carry bones to water or trees. Bones should then be kept in a suitable building, or, if that cannot be afforded, the dead man may be laid on the ground on a carpet and pillow, clothed with the light of heaven and beholding the sun.
is_a fargard It sets out rules concerning the Drug Nasu, death pollution, cleansing, healing, Dakhmas, fiends, still-born children, and defiled offerings.
Clothing is a covering for infirm persons in a Mazdean house. Touched by a corpse, it is defiled; cleansing may permit use for a sick woman or unfit man, never worshippers of Mazda.

l: worshippers of the Daêvas, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: are_treated_by art of healing [before worshippers of Mazda] A healer must first test his skill on them. If he causes three of them to die, he becomes permanently unfit to practise healing; if he heals three, he becomes fit to practise it.

l: art of healing, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Art of healing uses knife treatment, herbs, and most effectively the holy word; a healer qualifies after curing three Daêva worshippers and is permanently unfit after three patients die.

is_a fargard Fargard VIII sets out rules concerning dead dogs and men, corpse removal, purification, ritual penalties, sexual conduct, and the law of Mazda. It includes instructions attributed to Ahura Mazda on dealing with the Drug Nasu and the Daêva.

A grave, used when weather prevents immediate removal of the dead, is dug in the cleanest, driest, least-traveled place in the house. It is half a foot deep in hard earth or half a man’s height in soft earth, then covered with ashes or cowdung and dust.

l: building of clay, stones, and mortar, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: is_a place for corpses [raised where corpse-eating dogs and birds are always found] The corpse-bearers carry the body to a building of clay, stones, and mortar on a place where corpse-eating dogs and birds are always found.
Fiend-smiting words are ritual recitations by an Âthravan before corpse-bearing use and after purification, invoking the Lord and Mazda to smite the fiend and drive away the Drug.

Daêva is identified with a man who lies with mankind, as a worshipper and male paramour of the Daêvas, and as a Daêva in his inmost self and whole being. After death, one already a Daêva becomes an unseen Daêva.
A corpse-burning fire is handled by killing the burner, removing its cauldron and tripod, dispersing it in bundles, or bringing it to Dâityô-gâtu for fire-brands.
Dâityô-gâtu is a destination receiving several kinds of fire, with rewards measured in equivalent fire-brands according to the fire brought.
Fire-brands measure the posthumous rewards for bringing fires to the Dâityô-gâtu. The stated equivalents range from ten thousand for a corpse-burning fire to ten for a man's own hearth fire.

l: man who has touched a corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: A man who has touched a corpse must seek cleansing. He washes with gômêz, rubs dry, runs Hâthra until meeting or overtaking a man, and cries out for cleansing. If no man cleanses him after reaching habitation, he cleanses himself with gômêz and water. Finding water on the way incurs four hundred stripes with each instrument; refusing penalty and atonement leads him to inhabit the mansion of the Drug.

l: bringing fire to the Dâityô-gâtu, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Bringing fire to the Dâityô-gâtu is an event rewarded after a man’s soul has parted from his body. Its central feature is a graded reward of fire-brands based on the fire’s source: corpse-burning fire earns ten thousand, while his own hearth earns ten. Between these are fires from excrement, cowdung, kilns, reapers, craftspeople, ovens, cauldrons, encampments, herdsmen, and fields, with specified or source-dependent amounts. The event proceeds by bringing a particular fire, then receiving the corresponding reward after death.

l: cleansing after touching a corpse, Vendidad (Vendîdâd), Fargards I-VIII
s: Cleansing after touching a corpse involves washing with gômêz, rubbing dry, running until meeting or overtaking others, and calling aloud for cleansing. If others refuse, the man ultimately cleanses himself with gômêz and water.

These records summarize Fargards IX–XXII, a sequence of teachings in which Zarathustra repeatedly asks Ahura Mazda how to protect and restore the world against death, defilement, disease, demons, and wrongdoing. The account begins with the nine-night Barashnûm cleansing for contamination by the dead: prepared ground, holes, sprinkling, washing, recitations, seclusion, rewards for competent cleansers, and penalties for ignorant practice. Further sections prescribe sacred words, ritual spaces, and cleansing chants to repel the Drug Nasu, Aêshma, Angra Mainyu, and other harmful beings from people, homes, fire, water, earth, animals, and creation. It then regulates mourning, cleansing a bereaved household, and the treatment of dogs, especially water dogs. Killing or mistreating such animals brings major penalties; killing a water dog requires extensive restitution and atonement, with holiness or wickedness as the final consequence. Other laws identify grave, unatoned sins involving false teaching, harm to dogs or pregnant beings, sexual acts, miscarriage, and failure to support pregnant women and bitches. Menstruation, bodily emissions, hair, nails, and personal ritual observance are also governed by rules of distance, disposal, seclusion, cleansing, and punishment. Later teachings define an Âthravan and describe how Sraosha, Fire, Parôdars, sacred clothing, discipline, and atonement oppose Death and the Drug. Angra Mainyu’s attempt to destroy Zarathustra fails when Zarathustra recites the Ahuna-Vairya and refuses to abandon the good law. Ahura Mazda also explains the righteous soul’s crossing of the Kinvad bridge, guidance by the well-shapen maid, and arrival at Garô-nmânem, while the Daêvas retreat to hell. The sequence concludes with healing. Thrita is named the first healer, receiving remedies and opposing sickness, fever, death, and pain. Waters, heavenly lights, healing spells, Airyaman, Mãthra Spenta, and Nairyô-sangha are invoked to bring health, fertility, purification, and protection. Finally, after Angra Mainyu creates diseases, Airyaman arrives with animals and nine twigs, makes nine furrows, and drives away diseases, deaths, demons, and afflictions.
Fargard IX describes the nine-night Barashnûm ritual, its procedures, rewards, penalties, and consequences for those defiled by the dead.

is_a cleansing rite [lasting nine nights] The Barashnûm is a cleansing rite lasting nine nights for one defiled by the dead. It involves holes, furrows, gômêz, water, recitations, washing, and periods of seclusion.

Zarathustra is a holy, faithful, upright man, son of Pourusaspa, who serves the good law of the worshippers of Mazda and acts as a fiend-smiter against the Daêvas. He wields stones as big as a house, but regards the sacred Word as his best weapon. Across the records, he repeatedly asks Ahura Mazda for instruction: first on cleansing people defiled by the dead and fighting the Drug Nasu; then on cleansing houses, elements, living beings, and good creations; and on mourning and defilement. He also asks about penalties for killing a water dog, the handling of hair and nails, Death, Sraosha, grief to Ahura Mazda, atonement, sickness, death, fever, and healing. Ahura Mazda directs him in recitations, invocations, cleansing rites, and lawful practices. Zarathustra resists the Drug with the Ahuna-Vairya and steadfastly refuses to renounce the good law. The account closes with further instructions involving clouds, sickness and death, and Ahura Mazda addressing Spitama Zarathustra.

Ahura Mazda is the Holy One, a most beneficent and most knowing Spirit, and Maker of the material world, all good things, the dog, the aerial way, the earth, and a beautiful shining mansion seen afar. It matters most as a source of creation, healing, holiness, purity, and authoritative answers to Zarathustra and Spitama Zarathustra. It makes good things as offspring of the holy principle, makes the dog watchful, wakeful, sharp-toothed, and protective of human goods, brings down healing plants around Gaokerena, and invokes health upon mortal bodies. Across the records, Ahura Mazda explains cleansing rites, distances, measures, recitations, protections against fiends and defilement, mourning, dogs, sins, pregnancy, blood, discarded hair and nails, conduct, atonement, and the differing ends of holy and wicked people. It identifies Thrita as the first healer, makes growth occur through waters and light, and grants a boon for holiness. At the end, after Angra Mainyu afflicts it with diseases, Ahura Mazda seeks healing through Mãthra Spenta and Airyaman, offers sacrifices and a holy blessing-spell, and calls Nairyô-sangha to summon Airyaman.

Ahura Mazda is the Holy One and most beneficent Spirit, maker of the material world, creator of the good world, sacred Word in soul, and source ruling the worshippers’ good law. Rebels oppose the Lord. Ahura Mazda prescribes atonements for killing a water dog, then teaches Zarathustra protections, purification, worship, and souls’ fate after death.
A truth-speaking, learned godly man who knows Mazda’s cleansing rites is authorized to prepare the ground and perform cleansing.
The unclean one, defiled by the dead, undergoes Barashnûm cleansing through sprinkling, dust and water washing, seclusion, then final washing and restored approach after nine nights.

The faithful are Mazda worshippers, men and women. They must remain apart from cleansing grounds and unclean people during seclusion, and rejoice when cleansing from the Nasu is proper. They are promised gifts, rejoicing, desirable reward through the law, and holiness’ boon.

The worshippers of Mazda are faithful people governed by duties in Fargards IX, XV, and XVI. They reward lawful cleansing and punish ignorant cleansing; reject a foreign wrong creed knowingly taught as sin; and support every pregnant female. For a woman they clear and prepare a place, build shelter, provide food at a distance, wash her, kill specified Khrafstras, and do not suppress her issue.

Nasu is a Drug and defilement associated with Aêshma, rushing from the dead upon the living and defiling those who contact the dead. As gômêz is sprinkled, she moves from head to feet, is driven to the toes, and flies north as a raging fly. Prescribed words drive her from all places and the holy world; improper cleansing strengthens her.

Drug is a fiendish, wretched, wicked demon associated with defilement by the dead and identified as Bûiti and the unseen death. It rushes from the dead upon the living, defiling them and seeking to give the living world of the holy spirit to death. It becomes weaker or fades when prescribed Gâthic words and words that smite Angra Mainyu, Aêshma, the Mâzainya fiends, and all fiends are recited. It has progeny through four males: one who withholds treasured riches or refuses a small gift, one who urinates on the upper forepart of his foot, one who emits seed during sleep, and a person over fifteen without the sacred girdle or sacred shirt. Drug rushes to destroy Zarathustra but fears his glory, is dismayed by the Ahuna-Vairya, and flees. It is opposed by Zarathustra and the good creatures, smitten by invoked powers, and commanded to perish and depart with the brood and world of the fiend to the regions of the north, never again to give the living world unto death.

Angra Mainyu is a mischievous, deadly, guileful, evil-doing Daêva and ruffian, described as the maker of the evil world. He creates the evil world, makes Khrafstras, and by witchcraft brings disease, sickness, rottenness, and infection upon mortals. He opposes Zarathustra: he sends the Drug to destroy him and later urges him to renounce the good law, but Zarathustra refuses and names sacred things as weapons against Angra Mainyu and his creation. Prescribed words smite him down and drive him from houses through the whole holy world, from the defiled, and from fire, water, earth, living things, faithful people, heavenly lights, boundless light, and all good things made by Mazda. The afflictions he creates are also driven away.

l: Aêshma of the bloody spear, Vendidad (Vendîdâd)
s: A fiend smitten through repeated Ahuna-Vairya chanting, opposed by healing words that command it to perish and drive away its brood and world.
Mâzainya fiends are Daêvas smitten by recitation, armed with undedicated nails and opposed by dedicated nails.

Ashemaogha is an ungodly, wicked person who improperly cleanses an unclean one without knowing Mazda’s rites, causing sickness and death. While alive, he directly and indirectly defiles creatures of the good spirit, smites water, blows out fire, carries off the cow, kills or strikes the faithful man, and deprives him of necessities. The affected land and fields lack sweetness, health, healing, fulness, increase, and growth until he is put to death; once dead, he no longer commits these acts.

Sraosha is a holy, strong, tall-formed being and incarnate Word, armed with a club and invoked against fiends. After Ashemaogha’s death, sacrifice is offered for three days and nights. Sraosha brings clean wood to Fire, wakes Parôdars, questions the Drug, is worshipped with sacrifice, and smites Kunda.
Vohu-manô, a holy being with a golden seat, is defiled by the Daêvas and cleansed through washing, nine nights under heaven, and fire perfume.

Ârmaiti Spenta protects the faithful with Ahura Mazda, receives a man delivered by Sraosha for return at resurrection, is clad in grass partly withered by Gahi’s look, and restores the sleeper’s seed-emitting man as learned in sacred law.
A holy creation of Ahura Mazda, the material world risks sickness, death, and diminished fulness when cleansing is improper.
The whole holy world is included among the places and beings from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, defilement, and various fiends are driven away.
House is cleansed through prescribed washing, chanting, offerings, and libations; spoken words cleanse it, after which it becomes clean and admits waters, fire, and Amesha-Spentas.

is_a place for a woman who has an issue of blood The place of infirmity is where the woman sits while she continues to see blood after successive nights. She remains there until the prescribed number of nights has passed.

Fire is the son of Ahura Mazda, approached with worship and protected from uncleanness. It is kept thirty paces from the cleansing ground and fifteen paces from a woman who has an issue of blood; the unclean avoid it during nine nights of seclusion. Cleansing words drive Pairika and the demon of uncleanness away. Fire is fed dry, clean wood carried by well-washed hands, while an offender brings vast loads of hard, soft, or sweet-scented wood as atonement. During the night, Fire calls the master of the house, the husbandman, and then Sraosha, blessing whoever brings clean wood.

Water is a holy creation of Mazda, governed by ritual separation and cleansing. It must stand thirty paces from the cleansing ground and fifteen from a woman with an issue of blood. Washing proceeds through three earth holes once, twice, then three times; worship drives Pairika and uncleanness away.
Holy Ahura creation, earth bears people and Ahura’s women; worship and chanting cleanse it, driving away Pairika and uncleanness.

is_cleansed_by cleansing words [by chanting] The cow is cleansed through words ordering excellent deeds so that she may have a resting place and fodder. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the cow are driven away.

is_cleansed_by cleansing words [by chanting] The trees are cleansed by saying that Mazda made the plants grow through holiness. Pairika and the demon of uncleanness that come upon the tree are driven away.
Gômêz, a purifying substance from an ungelded bull, is sprinkled on the unclean one and used with water to cleanse bodies and clothes after seclusion.
The cleansing ground has six spaced holes and three more, surrounded by a knife-drawn furrow; the unclean one uses them in sprinkling and washes at the first three.
Fargard IX describes drawing twelve furrows around holes with a metal knife and placing hard matter as steps at intervals.
Yathâ ahû vairyô is a fiend-smiting, healing prayer recited during cleansing, teaching holiness as the Drug Nasu is driven away at six holes.

Ke verethrem gâ is a fiend-smiting, healing cleansing prayer recited after Gâthas; through named formulas and object-specific words, it cleanses a house and drives away fiends, defilement, uncleanness, and named daêvas.

are_known_by godly man [according to the law of Mazda] The rites of cleansing require knowledge of the law of Mazda and include preparing the ground, reciting words, sprinkling with gômêz, using dust and water, applying perfumes, and observing nine nights of seclusion.
Defilement by the dead is cleansed through the Barashnûm. A person defiled by the dead is considered dangerous to the purity of the world until the prescribed cleansing and seclusion are completed.

Cleansing is a ritual purification for one defiled by the dead. Proper cleansing delights the sun, moon, stars, fire, water, earth, cow, trees, and faithful, and earns the cleanser welfare in the blessed abode. Through prescribed words and repeated chants, it cleans the material world and drives away fiends, defilements, demons, and Angra Mainyu. House cleansing proceeds through three washings each of bodies and clothes, three Gâtha chants, sacrifice to Fire, baresma, and libations to good waters.

Sickness and death become stronger when a person who does not know the rites performs the cleansing. They threaten the land and fields until the improper cleanser is put to death and the required sacrifice to Sraosha is performed.
Health is invoked upon mortal bodies by blessing-spells, prayers, and praises, returning with sweetness and fatness after Ashemaogha’s death and sacrifice to Sraosha.

Daêvas are wicked, false-speaking evil-doing spirits, produced in the earth when hair or nails are improperly discarded; that deed increases their baleful strength. They cause persistent issue of blood, defile Vohu-manô through bodies they smite, make Âzi, and oppose Fire. They wither improperly clothed people over fifteen. Seeking Zarathustra’s death, they are repelled and flee to Arezûra and into hell.

are_a holy and beneficent chants [ruling over the ratus] The Gâthas contain words that are to be recited twice, thrice, or four times aloud. Specific passages from the Gâthas are listed for each number of repetitions.
The house is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.
The borough is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.
The town is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.
The land is among the places from which Angra Mainyu, Nasu, direct and indirect defilement, and various fiends are driven away.
The dead are the source from which the Drug and Nasu rush upon and defile the living.
The living are threatened by the Drug and Nasu, which rush from the dead and defile them. The final prayer asks that the living world no longer be given to death.
Purity is described as the greatest good for man next to life. It is obtained through the law of Mazda by cleansing oneself with good thoughts, words, and deeds.
The law of Mazda is a fiend-destroying law that procures purity through good thoughts, words, and deeds; Zarathustra steadfastly refuses to renounce it despite bodily, living, and spiritual ruin.

is will of the Lord The law of holiness is identified with the will of the Lord. The text connects it with protection, cleansing, the desirable reward, and the works through which the world may thrive.

l: good thoughts, good words, and good deeds, Vendidad (Vendîdâd)
s: Good thoughts, good words, and good deeds are three excellent things in which people must never be slack; they cleanse a person and win purity, while fire blesses one who brings clean wood.

Purification requires digging nine holes in the part of the ground where there is least water and where there are fewest trees, with nothing there that may be food for man or beast. A person can achieve purification by cleansing himself with good thoughts, words, and deeds.

Airyaman is a much-desired holy healer invoked for the faithful and the men and women of Zarathustra to bring rejoicing. He is called upon to smite or drive away all manner of disease, sickness, and death, as well as Yâtus, Pairikas, and wicked Gainis. In Fargards XX and XXI, the call emphasizes rejoicing and protection from these harms. In Fargard XXII, after receiving Ahura Mazda’s message through Nairyô-sangha, Airyaman comes with nine stallions, camels, bulls, head of small cattle, twigs, and furrows, then drives the evils away. He is associated with the mountain and forest of the holy questions, toward which he eagerly sets off.
Long-handed Bûshyãsta comes after the living world wakes, lulling it and urging people to sleep prematurely.
Faithful man’s soul is parted by Ashemaogha’s deadly blow, then he is cleansed through chanting, ritual materials and prayers over nine nights, and invocation of Airyaman for rejoicing and holiness.
The faithful woman is cleansed through chanting and ritual, calling beloved Airyaman so Zarathustra’s men and women rejoice in lawful reward and holiness.
Stars contain the seed of waters, rise above Hara Berezaiti, and produce light for the world.
The moon rises above Hara Berezaiti, produces light for the world, and keeps within itself the bull’s seed.
The swift-horsed sun rises above Hara Berezaiti, following Mazda’s path and the gods’ watery way to light the world.

l: all good things made by Mazda, Vendidad (Vendîdâd)
s: is_a offspring of the holy principle All good things made by Mazda, the offspring of the holy principle, are included among the things cleansed by the prescribed words. Angra Mainyu and the forces of uncleanness are driven away from them.
has_offspring all good things made by Mazda The holy principle is identified as the source of all good things made by Mazda. The chants seek to preserve and cleanse what is connected with it.

Ahuna-Vairya is a sacred, fiend-smiting and most-healing chanted prayer expressing that the Lord’s will is the law of holiness. In cleansing it is chanted at changing counts, after furrows are drawn, and two hundred times for Vohu-manô; Zarathustra chants it to repel the Drug as a weapon against Angra Mainyu and to preserve man.

Death is a hell-born, unseen force given to the living world by the holy spirit and made by Gaini. It ends a man's life when his time is over, after which Daêvas assail him and his soul enters Time's way. It sets mourning and cleansing duties, though a stranger's death does not defile creation like a living Ashemaogha. Death is driven back, commanded to depart, and ultimately prayed to be destroyed so healing may follow.

is_a chapter Fargard XII. sets out mourning periods for deaths among relatives and explains how the house is to be cleansed afterward. It also discusses the defilement caused by a living Ashemaogha and the lack of such defilement after his death.

Mourning for the dead is prescribed in Fargard XII by the deceased person’s relationship to the mourner and by whether the dead are righteous or sinners. It begins with thirty days for righteous parents or children and sixty days for sinners, and reaches six months or a year for the master or mistress of the house. The periods then shorten with more distant kin: grandparents or grandchildren, uncles or aunts, cousins, a cousin’s child, and a cousin’s grandchild. In each stated paired case, sinners receive the longer period; the final summary supplies paired periods for cousins and their descendants.

A stranger is a person who does not profess the true faith or true law; upon dying, such a person directly or indirectly defiles creation no more than a frog whose venom has dried up after being dead more than a year.
